edges.description: Activation through toll-like receptor 4 is what releases the cytokine. The two are separated because the cited study tests them separately: depleting the cells tests the first, inhibiting the cytokine the second.

TNF-alpha acts on its receptor on Bergmann glia, which release glutamate onto metabotropic receptors on the Purkinje cell. Each link in that chain was tested separately, in rat cerebellar slice and, for the glutamate step, in dissociated cortical astrocyte culture.

Recorded as INDIRECT because the step is not demonstrated: the source that describes both ends says there is a gap between them. The edge is drawn so the graph reaches the clinical syndrome, and the gap is a discussion rather than a hidden assumption.

Recorded as INDIRECT because the cited series report cognitive deficits at follow-up without establishing the step from the cerebellar lesion to them.

Headache with the ataxia is what marks the tiers in which the cerebellum is swollen. No cited source states the mechanism, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates: raised pressure in the posterior fossa is the obvious route and none of these papers measures it.
The other half of the pair that marks those tiers, and on the same footing: an association the cited sources report without measuring what lies between.
Swelling in the posterior fossa obstructs cerebrospinal fluid outflow. No cited source states the hydrodynamics; five of the twenty assert the association and the rest do not mention it.

nodes.description: Inflammation induced in the cerebellar cortex of a normal animal, which is the system every mechanistic step in the middle of this entry's chain comes from. It is not a model of this disease's trigger - no antecedent infection, no latent interval, no immune response directed at the cerebellum - and its authors say in a companion review that the animals were not ataxic.

nodes.description: The step that makes this disease immune-mediated rather than infectious. Five of the twenty cited sources name an immune mechanism; the rest describe the disease without one, and one of them calls the aetiology usually viral. It places the syndrome in the family of immune-mediated cerebellar ataxias, beside gluten ataxia, the paraneoplastic degenerations and opsoclonus-myoclonus. Which effector does the damage is not settled here: autoantibodies against several cerebellar targets are reported in individual patients, and whether any of them is pathogenic rather than a consequence of damage is an open question recorded in this entry's discussions.

nodes.description: The consequence of posterior fossa swelling, and the reason the fulminant tier may need cerebrospinal fluid diversion. Four cited sources call it obstructive hydrocephalus in those words. HPO's nearest narrower term is Noncommunicating hydrocephalus, HP:0010953, and the two are not the same concept: asked directly, OLS returns no exact synonym for that term at all, and HPO's own definition says the most common form of noncommunicating hydrocephalus is obstructive, which makes obstructive a subset rather than a synonym. The binding therefore stays at the parent and the preferred term carries the sources' word.

nodes.description: An infection, or rarely a vaccination, precedes the cerebellar syndrome by a latent interval of about a week. The interval is what makes the syndrome post-infectious rather than an infection of the cerebellum. No single organism defines it: the commonest trigger differs by era and population, and in a quarter of children none is identified.

evidence.reference_title: Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018.
evidence.snippet: A total of 20 cases (65% were vaccinated for varicella) were included, of which 70% were subcategorized as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 20% acute cerebellitis (AC), and 10% acute fulminant cerebellitis (AFC). An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related to varicella or were temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines.

This is the cellular state the rodent work converges on, and the point at which the model and the human disease part company: the animals became hyperexcitable and did not become ataxic, while the ataxic animal models in the same literature show Purkinje degeneration and hypoexcitability instead.

evidence.reference_title: Acute Cerebellar Inflammation and Related Ataxia: Mechanisms and Pathophysiology.
evidence.snippet: In our animal model of the acute inflammation of the cerebellar cortex, animals did not show any ataxia but hyperexcitability in the cerebellar cortex and depression-like behaviors. In contrast, animal models with neurodegeneration of the cerebellar Purkinje cells and hypoexcitability of the neurons show cerebellar ataxia. The suppression of the Ca2+-activated K+ channels in vivo is associated with a type of ataxia. Therefore, there is a gap in our interpretation between the very early phase of cerebellar inflammation and the emergence of cerebellar ataxia.

evidence.snippet: Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion.
